result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of the Altis at Olympia, describing votive offerings near the precinct of Pelops. He tells of Phormis's bronze horse that stallions lust after, compares it to a magician's marvel in Lydia, and lists statues of Hermes, bulls, a trophy and a Mendæan offering.

scenes.title: Offerings of Phormis
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the row of offerings near the enclosure of Pelops, including Phormis's horses and charioteers, and the inscription on the first.

scenes.title: The Horse Stallions Desire
scenes.summary: Pausanias reports the Elean tradition that stallions madly try to mount Phormis's ugly bronze horse, attributing it to a magician's cunning.

scenes.title: Lydian Magician's Fire
scenes.summary: Pausanias recalls a marvel he saw in Lydia, where a magician kindles wood on an altar without fire.

scenes.title: Hermes Statues and Bulls
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the offering of Lycortas showing Phormis fighting, the Hermes statues and the bronze bulls.

scenes.title: The Bull That Killed a Boy
scenes.summary: A boy struck his head on a bronze bull and died; the Eleans wished to remove it, but Delphi ordered expiation as for involuntary homicide.
scenes.stakes: The bull risks removal from the Altis as blood guilty.

scenes.title: Trophy and Mendæan Offering
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes the Elean trophy and the Mendæan statue dedicated after taking Sipte.

analysis.text: Pausanias catalogues offerings with attention to artists, inscriptions and odd local traditions, showing his interest in marvels and in correcting common attributions.
The offerings of Phormis show how Greek mercenaries and Sicilian tyrants used Panhellenic sanctuaries to display wealth and prestige.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says the bull's case was treated like involuntary homicide, showing that even objects could be subject to ritual purification.

language_notes.text: "Votive offerings" are gifts dedicated to a god in thanks or fulfilment of a vow; here they are statues set up in the sanctuary.
"Not in metre": the inscription is a verse couplet whose opening line, the name and origin, does not fit the verse rhythm.
"Cunning of a magician" means the effect is credited to sorcery, perhaps a charm or drug worked into the statue.
"Altis" is the sacred grove and precinct of Zeus at Olympia, where the temples and statues stood.
"Impetuosity" means rash, violent eagerness; the stallions show more of it for the statue than for real mares.
The 'horse of Phormis' is the bronze horse offering discussed just before, which Pausanias also called a magician's trick (a device said to frighten mares).
'Lydians called Persici' were Lydians settled under Persian rule, who kept Persian-style fire worship; Hierocæsarea and Hypæpa were cities in Lydia, in Asia Minor.
A tiara was a soft Persian-style headdress, here part of the magician's ritual dress.
Pausanias often wanders from his main subject, then closes the 'digression' with a formula like this before returning to Olympia.
Greek law and religion treated even accidental killing as polluting, requiring purification; the bull is treated like an involuntary killer. Altis is the sacred precinct of Olympia.
Pausanias refers to a battle between Eleans and Lacedæmonians (Spartans) fought in the Altis; the roof repair brought the armed body to light in his own time.
'Dumb-bells' are halteres, stone or metal weights held by jumpers in the pentathlum to increase their leap.
The statue speaks in the first person ('put me here'), as inscribed objects commonly did. Zeus is the name this translation gives in the inscription.

context_notes.text: Gelon, tyrant of Syracuse, and his brother Hiero, who succeeded him, ruled Sicily in the early fifth century BC. Mercenaries like Phormis could rise high in their service.
Argos and Aegina were noted bronze-casting centres, so naming the sculptors tells the reader these were respected artists.
Hermes was the messenger god, often shown carrying a ram as protector of flocks. Pheneos was an Arcadian city.
Onatas of Ægina was a famous early fifth-century BC bronze sculptor, often mentioned by Pausanias.
The pentathlum was the five-event contest of the games: running, jumping, discus, javelin and wrestling.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias gives his own rationalizing judgment, mixing reported local tradition with a guide's cautious opinion.
The ugly, tailless statue attracts stallions more than living mares, a comic contrast with its plain appearance.
Slipping hoofs, fierce neighing and whips make a vivid, almost comic picture of frantic animal desire.
The vivid picture of wood igniting without fire and a bright blaze conveys the wonder Pausanias felt and supports his claim to eyewitness.
The innocent description of the boy at play, with the sudden movement, prepares for the abrupt, unexpected death reported at the end.
Pausanias admits to being nearly deceived, a candid personal touch that shows him as an observant, fallible traveler.
